title: Two Pointers: Remove the Nth Node From the End
oneLiner: Start two pointers at a dummy node, move the lead n + 1 steps ahead, then move both until the lead falls off the end: the trailing pointer is right before the node to delete.
keyTakeaway: "n from the end" becomes "n behind a pointer that reaches the end". Keep a fixed gap between two pointers and walk them together, and you never need the list's length. A dummy node in front of head means removing the head itself is not a special case.
explanation:
Given the head of a singly linked list and n, remove the n-th node counting from the end (n = 1 is the last node) and return the head of the result. n is always between 1 and the list's length. The two-pass answer counts the length L, then walks to node L - n. The two-pointer answer does it in one pass.

To delete a node from a singly linked list you need the node BEFORE it, so you can set before.Next = before.Next.Next. The trick is to get a pointer to that node without knowing L. Put both pointers, lead and trail, on a dummy node whose Next is head. Move lead n + 1 steps forward. Now there are exactly n nodes between trail and lead. Move both one step at a time until lead is null (it has walked off the end). The gap hasn't changed, so trail is now n + 1 steps before the end, which is the node right before the one to remove. Unlink it and return dummy.Next.

The dummy node matters when n equals the length: the node to remove is head itself, and without a node in front of it there's no "before" to rewire. With the dummy, trail simply stays on the dummy and dummy.Next becomes the second node. Return dummy.Next, not head, because head may be the node you just removed.

The same fixed-gap idea answers "return the k-th node from the end" and is a cousin of the fast and slow pointers: both pointers move at the same speed here, and what does the work is the head start.

In the visualization the first node is the dummy. The pointer labeled fast is the lead and slow is the trail.

recognitionSignals: A position counted from the END of a singly linked list ("n-th from last", "k-th to last") and you'd rather not count the length first.
"Do it in one pass" on a linked list where the answer depends on how far a node is from the tail.
You need to delete or insert a node that might be the head, which is when a dummy node saves a special case.
gotchas: Off by one: to stop on the node BEFORE the target, the lead starts n + 1 steps ahead of the trail (both starting at the dummy). With a gap of n the trail lands on the target itself, and you can't unlink a node from itself.
Return dummy.Next, not head; when n equals the length, head is the node that got removed.
Without a dummy, removing the head needs its own branch, and forgetting it is the most common bug here.

complexity.note: The lead pointer walks the list once and the trail pointer follows it, so each node is visited at most twice in a single pass; only the dummy node and two pointers are extra.

referenceSolutions.python:
def remove_nth_from_end(head, n):
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)  # so removing head isn't a special case
    lead = trail = dummy
    for _ in range(n + 1):  # n + 1 steps ahead
        lead = lead.next
    while lead is not None:
        lead = lead.next
        trail = trail.next
    trail.next = trail.next.next  # trail is just before the n-th node from the end
    return dummy.next
